newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Farm leader says EU reform plans catastrophic.
newsitem.headline: Farm leader says EU reform plans catastrophic.

text.p: European Commission draft plans to slash farm support prices with only partial compensation for lost earnings would be disastrous, Europe's farmers said on Friday .
The EU proposal, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters on Tuesday, envisaged cuts in guaranteed beef, cereals and dairy prices of between 10 and 30 percent.
Cereals farmers, whom the EU Commission believes have been heavily over-paid in recent years, would only be compensated for half the reduction.
"If the proposal is fully implemented it would have a catastrophic impact on farmers' revenues," Luc Guyau, President of the EU farmers' organisation, COPA, told a news briefing.

Guyau, who is also head of the main French farmers' union FNSEA, said farmers had not been consulted and that there could be demonstrations if their views were not taken into account and new proposals drafted.
"Systematic price cuts are unacceptable if they destroy farmers earnings and are not compensated," he said.

The farm reforms are part of a package of measures to prepare for EU enlargement eastwards which EU Commission President Jacques Santer is due to unveil to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Wednesday.
The reforms, which continue down the same path taken in 1992, are intended to prevent grain and beef mountains reappearing and to keep spending under control.
"It's unacceptable to sacrifice farmers in order to save the budget," a Swedish farmers' official said, adding that the draft plans harmed the environment, animal welfare and food safety.

Guyau admitted that farmers had issued similar warnings when radical reforms, including a one third cut in cereals support prices, were proposed in 1992 but subsequently found that the impact was not so bad.

Farm incomes have since increased by an average of 4.5 percent a year, but Guyau said this was due to a sharp decline in the number of farmers and higher prices due to drought in Australia and surging Chinese imports.
"Our wish is to keep farmers on the land fulfilling various roles," Guyau said, stressing that farmers played important roles in protecting the countryside and keeping rural areas vibrant.
World prices should not be the benchmark for the EU, he said, stressing that European farmers had to meet higher environmental and social standards.

Guyau was cautious about Commission plans to limit payments to individual farms so as to ensure a fairer distribution of aid. About 80 percent of EU farm subsidies are paid to only 20 percent of farmers, mainly the so-called grain barons.
"We want to avoid excesses and to be better understood by consumers, but we don't want to upset the balance between product sectors," he said.
